PREVIEW ONLY — not the AWeber render. Subject: 🪙 {{ subscriber.first_name | capitalize }}, wear it on your left wrist. I'll explain why.  ·  Preheader: One instruction, before you even know what it is.
 

{{ subscriber.first_name | capitalize }}, before I tell you what it is — left wrist, never right

I'm not going to lead with the reading tonight. I'm going to lead with the one instruction that matters, and let the reading explain itself after.

{{ subscriber.first_name | capitalize }} —

Evelyn here.

Something is coming to you, and before you know what it is, I need you to know how to hold it.

When it reaches you: left wrist. Not your right. I'll tell you why by the end of this letter, and I'd rather you carry the instruction the whole way there than wait for it at the finish.

Here's how I know something is coming at all.

I keep a canister of temple sticks on the shelf above where I read. Thirty-six of them, numbered, kept there more out of habit these days than use — I reach for cards for almost everyone who writes to me, because cards are what I know best.

But there's a small number of readings a year cards simply won't take. They sit there, and nothing comes, and I've learned not to force it.

Last night I was closing up, reaching past the canister for something else, and I knocked it without meaning to.

One stick came clean out onto the table. Not the whole handful — one, on its own, before I'd touched it properly.

I've stopped arguing with that kind of thing, dear. When something falls out on its own, it's already decided who it's for.

So I did what I do when that happens. I picked the canister up properly, and I asked it your question three times.

Here's how I want you to read what's below. The first two shakes are good news, and you're allowed to keep them exactly as they are.

Then read the third one twice.

And read all three of them as close. This isn't a fortune about some far year of your life — the shape of the third one is already active, and by my reckoning the next thing it's warning about lands inside a fortnight if it isn't addressed. That's why I didn't wait for morning to write to you.

The last time a stick came out at me like that, it was years ago — a woman named Frances, who wrote to me about money the way most people write to me about a man.

She let me shake it through properly.

Nothing arrived for her that hadn't already been arriving, if I'm honest with you. That's not what changed. What changed is that the amount stopped shrinking on its way to her — the same work, the same clients, the same modest good luck she'd always had, except now it stayed the size it came in at instead of going soft around the edges by the time it reached her account.

She didn't get richer overnight, dear. She got to keep what she was already owed.

I'll show you all three shakes in a moment, {{ subscriber.first_name | capitalize }}.

But you should know what you're holding first.

A single stick answers a single question, put through one door at a time — money, a man, health, travel, they're all separate doors and the same stick answers each one differently depending which you knock on. I asked yours through the money door, three times, which is more than I do most nights for anybody.

What I haven't done yet is the second stage — the proper temple reading, where the number is matched against what it's actually pointing at in your life rather than what it says on its own. That takes your say-so, because it isn't something I do to a stranger's question. It's something I do with someone who's asked me to.

So here's your three.

The first shake: stick six

I won't pretend I know why the numbers land the way they do. I only know what comes up when they do, and stick six is a good one to draw.

Its poem is a river poem — water that's already found its way down toward the sea and doesn't ask the sea's permission to arrive. When it comes up first, it says one thing plainly. Something that's owed to you is already moving, and it was moving before you asked me to look.

That's not hope, dear, that's the reading. Whatever's been slow, whatever's been "still pending", it hasn't stalled — it's in motion, the way a river is in motion even on the stretches where it looks flat from the bank.

What stick six won't tell me is what happens to it on the way. A river reaches the sea. It doesn't promise every drop of it gets there.

The second shake: stick eleven

Stick eleven's poem is a boat at a dock with two ropes — one at the bow, one at the stern — and only one of them still cleated down.

Coming second, this one carries a fork I can't resolve for you, and I want to be straight about why. I asked this stick through the money door. But eleven is one of the ones that reads differently depending which door it's asked through, and money and the door right next to it — what's happening with a particular man, or a marriage — answer this stick in opposite directions.

If money is tangled up with a person for you right now — and dear, for a great many of the women who write to me, it is — this stick is telling you something different than it would if it weren't. One rope being cut loose is either you're finally free to move, or something that was holding steady is coming undone, and from where I'm sitting I genuinely cannot tell you which rope is yours.

The full reading tells me which. A single shake, on its own, can't.

The third shake: stick seventeen

I don't love this one and I'm not going to pretend otherwise.

Stick seventeen's poem is a fisherman's poem too, on the surface — a full net, hauled in, a good catch. Every other line of it reads as good news, right up until the last: the fish is caught, but the net is torn.

Read that again, because it isn't saying what it sounds like it's saying. It isn't "you caught nothing." It's the opposite. You caught plenty. You've been catching for a long time, and I don't think anyone's ever once told you that the catching was never your problem.

The net is the problem. Somewhere in it there's a hole you've never been shown, and everything you land goes through it eventually — not all at once, not dramatically, just steadily, the way water finds the one gap in anything and takes it.

Here's what most people get wrong about a reading like this one. They think the fix is a bigger net, or a better spot to fish from — attract more, try harder, cast wider.

It isn't. A bigger net with the same hole in it just loses more, faster.

What seventeen is actually asking for isn't more catch. It's a seal.

So let me take this to the second stage, dear, and I'll show you exactly where your net is torn, and what closes it.

In concrete terms, what do you do now?

Nothing complicated.

You give me permission to finish the reading. That's the whole of it. I don't take a stick to its second stage without being asked — that isn't mine to do uninvited, and the first stage was already more than I let myself do on most nights.

Back to stick eleven, and the rope that's still cleated

I want to say plainly what I think is tied to that second rope, {{ subscriber.first_name | capitalize }}, because I've sat with it since last night.

It's not always a man. For a lot of the women who write to me it is — but just as often it's a person who was never romantic at all: a parent she's still propping up, a friend she keeps lending to, a version of herself from ten years ago she hasn't let go of financially. The rope holds because letting it go feels like a betrayal of someone, even when the someone is her.

The second stage tells me which rope is doing the holding in your case, and whether it's the one worth cutting or the one worth keeping.

Let me finish the reading and I'll tell you which.

And back to seventeen — this is the part I want you to sit with

Here's what seventeen is actually warning you about, dear. It isn't the losing.

It's the not noticing.

A torn net doesn't announce itself. Nothing rips open all at once, and nobody stands over a fishing boat watching the exact stitch give way. It just quietly fishes worse every season, and by the time anyone checks the net, they've long since stopped remembering what a full one used to feel like.

You've been fishing this way long enough that "some of it goes missing" has started to feel normal to you. I don't think it should.

Finish the reading with me, and I'll show you exactly where the tear is — not generally. Where.

Why I told you the wrist before I told you anything else

Every other reading I do ends the same way I do it — with words. More cards, a longer letter, a fuller explanation.

This one can't, and that's the real reason I opened with an instruction instead of a story.

A torn net isn't fixed by being told about it. You can describe a hole in a net as precisely as you like and the water still gets through while you're talking. What closes a hole is something physical, sitting exactly where the hole is, for as long as it needs to.

That's why the second stage of this reading ends with something you wear rather than something you read. And that's why the wrist matters: the left hand is the one that receives, nearer the heart, the one that takes rather than gives. Worn on the right, you'd be offering the seal to what you're sending out, not what's reaching you — which is the one way to take a thing built to stop a leak and make it feed one instead.

I'll tell you exactly what it is, and where it comes from, once you've asked me to finish. It's older than my own deck, and it comes from a tradition that doesn't read the way tarot does — which is a large part of why I reached for sticks instead of cards for you in the first place. You don't read an old kind of leak with a new kind of instrument.

Come back to me here and let me finish it properly

I'm not going to tell you this fixes money. It doesn't put anything in front of you that wasn't already coming — I want to be honest about that, because seventeen was clear on the point and I'm not going to soften it for the sake of the letter.

Here's what it does do.

What already reaches you stops leaking back out before you've had the chance to close your hand around it. The catching was never the part that needed help. This is for the part after.

Finish the reading whenever you're ready.

I'm on your side in this, dear.

— Evelyn

## P.S. (ships on every letter — settled 2026-08-10, no A/B)

P.S. If you take nothing else from tonight, take the line from seventeen: the fish is caught, but the net is torn. That isn't a bad draw, dear — it's the first honest look you've had at where it's actually going. The second stage is here whenever you want it.
